lessons.title: Is Rust object-oriented?
lessons.objective_md: See which object-oriented ideas Rust has (objects, encapsulation, polymorphism) and how it replaces inheritance.

screens.heading: Objects: data plus behaviour
screens.text_md: A common definition says an **object** packages data with the procedures that operate on it. By that definition Rust has objects: a struct holds the data, and its `impl` block holds the methods. Rust just doesn't call them objects.

coming_from.c: Like a C++ class or a C struct with functions, where privacy is per module, not per class.
coming_from.go: Very close to Go: structs with methods, no inheritance, and interfaces (traits) for polymorphism.
coming_from.java: Like a class with private fields and public methods, minus inheritance: there's no `extends`.
coming_from.js: Like a class, but data (the struct) and methods (the `impl`) are written separately, and there's no prototype chain.
coming_from.python: A struct with an `impl` block plays the role of a class. There's no `__init__`; a `new` function is just a convention.

Not quite. Fields are private by default.

screens.heading: Reaching into private fields
screens.text_md: The compiler enforces the boundary (**E0616**). Because no outside code can set `value` directly, the module's own methods are the only place where its rules need checking.

screens.heading: No inheritance: traits and composition
screens.text_md:
Rust has no **inheritance**: a struct can't extend another struct and pick up its fields. Two tools cover what inheritance is used for:

- **Shared behaviour:** a trait's default methods (`describe`) are reused by every implementor, and any implementor can override them.
- **Shared data:** put one struct inside another as a field (composition) and forward to it.

lessons.title: Trait objects
lessons.book_section: 18.2 Using Trait Objects to Abstract over Shared Behavior
lessons.objective_md: Store values of different types behind one trait, with `Box<dyn Trait>` and `&dyn Trait`, and call their methods.

screens.heading: A `Vec` holds one type
screens.text_md: Both types can draw, but a `Vec` needs one element type (**E0308**). A GUI library wants exactly this, though: a list of components whose types it doesn't know in advance.
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0308]: mismatched types
  --> src/main.rs:22:30
   |
22 |     let items = vec![Button, Label];
   |                              ^^^^^ expected `Button`, found `Label`

annotations.note_md: line 22: every element of a `Vec` must have the same type.

screens.heading: `Box<dyn Draw>`
screens.text_md:
A **trait object**, written `dyn Draw`, stands for "some type that implements `Draw`". Its size isn't known, so it always lives behind a pointer: `Box<dyn Draw>` owns one, `&dyn Draw` borrows one.

Every `Box<dyn Draw>` has the same type, so they share a `Vec`. Calling `draw` runs the method of whichever type is inside the box.

coming_from.c: Like `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Drawable>>` with virtual functions; the vtable lives in the fat pointer, not the object.
coming_from.go: Like a `[]Drawer` slice of interface values: each holds a pointer and a method table.
coming_from.java: Very close to `List<Drawable>` with an interface type: each call goes through a method table.
coming_from.js: Like `Array<Drawable>` where `Drawable` is an interface; the check happens at compile time.
coming_from.python: Like a list of objects that all have a `draw` method (duck typing), except the compiler checks that each one implements `Draw`.

question.prompt_md: Why must a trait object such as `dyn Draw` be behind a pointer like `Box` or `&`?

options.text_md: Its size isn't known at compile time, since it could be any implementing type.
Trait objects are always on the heap.
It doesn't need one; `Vec<dyn Draw>` works.

explanations.text_md: Correct. A pointer has a known size, whatever it points at.
Not quite. `&dyn Draw` can point at a value on the stack.
Not quite. The pointer is about size, not speed.
Not quite. `dyn Draw` alone is unsized.

screens.heading: Borrowing a trait object
screens.text_md: A function that only needs to call methods can take `&dyn Draw`. No boxing or allocation is needed: `&ok` becomes a trait object reference automatically, and `ok` is still usable afterwards.

screens.heading: Open to new types
screens.text_md: `Screen` was written without knowing `SelectBox` exists. Any type that implements `Draw`, including types defined later in other crates, can go in the screen. This openness is what trait objects give over an enum, whose variants are fixed when it's written.

question.prompt_md: A `Vec<Box<dyn Draw>>` can hold types that were written after the code that uses the vector.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Any implementor of `Draw` fits.
Not quite. That openness is the point of trait objects.

screens.heading: Mutating through a trait object
screens.text_md: Methods taking `&mut self` work through trait objects too: `iter_mut` gives `&mut Box<dyn Stage>`, so each stage can update its own fields. The `Counter` remembers how many times it has run.

lessons.title: Static vs dynamic dispatch, and dyn compatibility
lessons.objective_md: Tell static from dynamic dispatch, and know which traits can be used as `dyn` trait objects.

screens.heading: Static dispatch
screens.text_md: A generic function is **monomorphized**: the compiler writes a separate copy of `twice` for `Cat` and for `Cow`, and each copy calls the right `speak` directly. Choosing the method at compile time is **static dispatch**. It can be inlined and optimised, at the cost of a little more compiled code.

coming_from.c: Generics are like templates (static dispatch); `dyn Trait` is like virtual functions.
coming_from.go: Go generics and interfaces exist too; Rust's generic code is fully specialised per type.
coming_from.java: Java generics are erased and calls are virtual; Rust generics are specialised per type (like C# generics over structs).
coming_from.js: JavaScript always dispatches dynamically. Rust generics are more like code specialised per type.
coming_from.python: Python always looks methods up at run time. Rust lets you choose: generics resolve at compile time, `dyn` at run time.

screens.heading: Dynamic dispatch
screens.text_md:
Here there's one `twice`. A `&dyn Speak` is a **fat pointer**: a pointer to the value and a pointer to its type's **vtable**, a table of the type's methods. Each call looks `speak` up in that table while the program runs: **dynamic dispatch**.

It's slightly slower (an indirect call the compiler can't inline) but it allows mixed types in one array and keeps the compiled code smaller.

question.prompt_md: When does a call through `&dyn Speak` decide which `speak` to run?

options.text_md: At run time, by looking it up in the vtable.
Never; it always calls the first implementation.

explanations.text_md: Correct. That's dynamic dispatch.
Not quite. That's what generics do.
Not quite. The choice depends on the value at run time.
Not quite. It calls the value's own implementation.

screens.heading: A trait that can't be a `dyn`
screens.text_md:
Not every trait can become a trait object. A trait is **dyn compatible** only if a vtable can be built for it. The main rules for each method:

- It doesn't return `Self` or take `Self` by value in other positions.
- It has no generic type parameters.
- It takes `self` in some form (`&self`, `&mut self`, `self: Box<Self>`…).

`duplicate` breaks the first rule (**E0038**).
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0038]: the trait `Shape` is not dyn compatible
  --> src/main.rs:19:25
   |
19 |     let shapes: Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> = vec![Box::new(Square(2))];
   |                         ^^^^^^^^^ `Shape` is not dyn compatible
   |
note: for a trait to be dyn compatible it needs to allow building a vtable

annotations.note_md: line 19: `duplicate` returns `Self`, and through a `dyn Shape` the compiler wouldn't know what type, or size, that is.

question.prompt_md: A trait with a method `fn make() -> Self;` (no `self` parameter) can be used as `dyn Trait` as it stands.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. There's no value to dispatch on, and `Self` is unknown.
Correct. Mark it `where Self: Sized` to keep the trait dyn compatible.

screens.heading: `where Self: Sized` keeps a method off the vtable
screens.text_md: `where Self: Sized` says the method only exists for types with a known size. `dyn Shape` isn't sized, so the method is left out of the vtable and the rest of the trait works as a trait object. On a concrete `Square`, `duplicate` still works.

screens.heading: Choosing between them
screens.text_md: Use **generics** when each call works with one type: they're fastest and keep full type information. Use **trait objects** when one collection or variable must hold different types, or the set of types is open-ended. `show_all_dyn` can mix an integer, a string and a float; `show_all_generic` can't.

question.prompt_md: Fill in the blank to keep `make` out of the vtable.
question.general_md: `where Self: Sized` excludes `make` from `dyn Thing`. The program prints `1`.

wrong_answers.why_md: that doesn't make the trait dyn compatible.

summary: Generics use static dispatch: one compiled copy per type, calls resolved at compile time.
Trait objects use dynamic dispatch: a fat pointer carries a vtable, and calls are looked up at run time.
A trait is dyn compatible when a vtable can be built: no `Self` returns, no generic methods, a `self` receiver.
`where Self: Sized` keeps an incompatible method on the trait but off the vtable.

lessons.title: The state pattern with trait objects
lessons.objective_md: Build the Book's blog post with the state pattern: state objects that decide their own transitions.

screens.heading: The workflow from outside
screens.text_md:
A blog post starts as a **draft**, goes to **review**, and is then **published**. Only a published post shows its text. From the outside, `Post` has just a few methods; it hides which state it's in.

The **state pattern** puts each state's behaviour in its own type, and the post delegates to whichever state it currently holds.

coming_from.c: Like the State pattern with `std::unique_ptr<State>`, where each transition returns the next pointer.
coming_from.go: Like an interface field swapped for a new value on each transition.
coming_from.java: The classic GoF State pattern: an interface, one class per state, and a context that delegates.
coming_from.js: Like swapping a `state` object that implements an interface, but ownership guarantees the old state can't be reused.
coming_from.python: The same pattern as in Python: a post object holding a state object whose class changes. Rust makes each transition consume the old state.

screens.heading: States as trait objects
screens.text_md:
The post holds its state as `Option<Box<dyn State>>`. Each transition method takes **`self: Box<Self>`**: it consumes the boxed state and returns the next one. A `Draft` asked for review becomes a `PendingReview`; a `PendingReview` asked again stays as it is (`self`).

`take()` moves the state out of the `Option` (leaving `None` for a moment), so it can be consumed and replaced.

question.prompt_md: Why is the state stored as `Option<Box<dyn State>>` rather than `Box<dyn State>`?

options.text_md: So `take()` can move the old state out through `&mut self` before replacing it.
Because a post may have no state at all.
Because trait objects must be optional.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Rust won't leave a field empty, so `Option` provides the temporary `None`.
Not quite. A post always has a state between calls.
Not quite. Boxes are never `Copy`.
Not quite. `Option` is a tool for the transition, not a rule.

screens.heading: Only published posts show text
screens.text_md:
`Post::content` asks its state. The trait's **default** `content` returns `""`, so `Draft` and `PendingReview` need no code for it; only `Published` overrides it. The lifetime `'a` says the text borrowed from `post` lives as long as the post, not the state.

(The Book writes `self.state.as_ref().unwrap()`; the course avoids `unwrap()` with a `match`.)

screens.heading: Adding a transition
screens.text_md: To add `reject`, declare it on the trait and give every state an answer. Only `PendingReview` really changes; `Draft` and `Published` return `self`. The rules about which transitions are allowed live entirely inside the states. `Post` just forwards the request.

question.prompt_md: In the state pattern, calling `approve` on a draft is a compile error.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. Every state has every method; a draft's `approve` simply returns `self`.
Correct. Invalid requests are handled at run time. L18.5 shows how to make them compile errors.

screens.heading: Trade-offs
screens.text_md:
The state pattern keeps each state's rules in one place, and new states can be added without changing `Post`. The costs:

- States know about each other (`Draft` creates `PendingReview`), so they're coupled.
- Mistakes such as approving a draft are silently ignored at run time rather than caught by the compiler.

lessons.title: Encoding states as types
lessons.book_section: 18.3 Encoding States and Behavior as Types
lessons.objective_md: Make each state its own type so the compiler rejects invalid transitions.

screens.heading: One type per state
screens.text_md: Instead of one `Post` with a hidden state, there's a **type per state**. `Post::new()` returns a `DraftPost`, and `DraftPost` has no `content` method at all. Reading a draft's text isn't a run-time "return an empty string"; it's a method that doesn't exist.

coming_from.c: Like returning different types from each step so misuse fails to compile, with moves making the old value unusable.
coming_from.go: Go can return different struct types per step, but can't stop you reusing the old value; Rust's moves can.
coming_from.java: Like a step builder or fluent interface where each step returns a different interface type.
coming_from.js: Like a builder whose steps return different TypeScript types, so the editor won't offer invalid methods.
coming_from.python: Like returning a different class from each step; Python would only catch a wrong call at run time, Rust at compile time.

screens.heading: Transitions consume the old state
screens.text_md: `request_review(self)` takes the draft **by value** and returns a `PendingReviewPost`; `approve(self)` turns that into a `Post`. Each step moves the text into the next type, and the old value is gone. Shadowing with `let post = …` keeps the name while the type changes.

options.text_md: It doesn't compile: `DraftPost` has no `content` method.

explanations.text_md: Correct. The error comes from the compiler.
Not quite. That's the state-object version.
Not quite. Nothing reaches run time.
Not quite. Drafts can't show text.

screens.heading: Using a state after it moved
screens.text_md: Ownership finishes the job (**E0382**). Once a draft is sent for review it no longer exists, so it can't be edited behind the reviewer's back. The state-object version would have to check this at run time.

annotations.mark: `draft` moved due to this method call
annotations.note_md: line 6: `request_review` took the draft by value.

screens.heading: Going back a step
screens.text_md: A rejection is just another consuming method, `PendingReviewPost::reject(self) -> DraftPost`. Transitions can go in any direction you design; what can't happen is calling a transition that the current type doesn't have.

question.prompt_md: With states as types, code that holds "a post in any state" in one variable is easier than with state objects.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. Each state is a different type, so one variable can't hold any of them without an enum or a trait object.
Correct. That's the trade-off; a post read from a file or a script suits state objects better.

screens.heading: Which design to choose
screens.text_md:
Three ways to model states, each with a place:

- **Type-state:** invalid transitions don't compile. Best when the sequence is in the code.
- **State objects:** open to new states, decided at run time. Best when states are driven by data.
- **An enum:** a closed set, checked with `match`. Best when the states are fixed and few.

Rust supports object-oriented patterns, but its own tools often encode the rules more directly.

problems.description_md:

problems.title: Maintain cached aggregate state
problems.description_md:
An `AveragedCollection` keeps a list of `i32` values and, so that `average` is cheap, a running `sum` of them. Both fields are private: if code outside could push to the list without updating the sum, the cached sum would be wrong.

Write the methods:

- `add(value)` pushes the value and updates the sum.
- `remove()` removes the last value and returns it (`None` when empty), updating the sum.
- `average()` returns `Some(sum / count)` as an `f64`, or `None` when the collection is empty. It must use the cached sum, not add the list up again.
- `len()` returns the number of values.

The sum is an `i64`, so it can't overflow for any number of `i32` values these tests use.

```text
Expression: { let mut c = crate::AveragedCollection::new(); for v in [1, 2, 3, 4] { c.add(v); } c.average() }
```

problems.title: Blog workflow, two ways
problems.comes_after: All chapter lessons and one Medium Accepted
problems.description_md:
Build the Book's blog post workflow twice, in the library package `blog`, and then drive it from a small script language. A post is written as a draft, sent for review, and either approved (published) or rejected (back to draft). Only a published post shows its text.

**Part 1 · State objects**

`Post` keeps its state as a private `Option<Box<dyn State>>`. `new`, `add_text`, `content`, `request_review`, `approve` and `reject` work as in L18.4: `reject` sends a post under review back to draft, and every request that doesn't apply leaves the state unchanged. `status()` returns `"draft"`, `"pending"` or `"published"`.

**Part 2 · State types**

The module `typed` has the same workflow as separate types: `typed::Post::new()` returns a `DraftPost`; `DraftPost::add_text` and `DraftPost::request_review(self) -> PendingReviewPost`; `PendingReviewPost::approve(self) -> Post` and `PendingReviewPost::reject(self) -> DraftPost`; `typed::Post::content`. Invalid requests don't exist: there's simply no such method.

**Part 3 · Scripts**

`run(script)` runs one command per line against a single state-object `Post`, and returns the output:

- `add TEXT` appends `TEXT` (everything after `add `) to the post.
- `review`, `approve`, `reject` request those transitions.
- `status` prints `status: STATE`.
- `show` prints `content: TEXT` (an empty string unless published).
- Blank lines are skipped. Any other command prints `line N: unknown command WORD`, where `N` counts every line from 1 and `WORD` is the line's first word, and the script carries on.

Each printed line ends with `\n`.
hints: Add `PendingReview` and `Published` states; only `Published` overrides `content`, and only `PendingReview` has real `approve` and `reject` transitions.
In `typed`, each transition moves `self.content` into the next struct.
In `run`, `line.split_once(' ')` separates the command from the rest; `add` uses the rest as the text, and `line.split_whitespace().next()` gives the word to report.
problems.solution_approach_md: Part 1 puts the rules inside the states: `Post` takes its boxed state, hands it to a consuming transition and stores the result. Part 2 moves the same rules into the type system: a draft has no `approve` method at all, so the invalid call can't be written. Part 3 needs a value that can be in *any* state at run time, read from a script, which is exactly what the state-object version is for.
problems.idiomatic_md: The two designs make different promises: state objects check the rules while the program runs and can be driven by data; state types check them while it compiles but need the sequence to be known in the code.
problems.random_md: For each case draw `n = pick(10)` lines; each is chosen by `pick(7)` from `add a`, `add é`, `review`, `approve`, `reject`, `status`, `show`, and lines are joined by `\n`. The case's result is `crate::run(script)`. Use the course generator, seed `0x12010000`, exactly 300 cases.

problems.title: Event plugins
problems.description_md:
The library can now notify plugins when something happens. The starter is the LM17 workspace with one new module, `core/src/plugins.rs` (`pub mod plugins;` is already in `core/src/lib.rs`). The rest of the library is unchanged.

**Part 1 · Events and plugins**

An `Event` is one of `Added { book_id, title }`, `CheckedOut { book_id, member_id }` or `Returned { book_id, fee_cents }`. A `Plugin` has a `name()` and an `on_event(&mut self, event)` that may return a message. `Plugin` has `Send` as a supertrait, so a library holding plugins can still move between threads. Write three plugins:

- `Announcer` (name `announcer`): for `Added`, the message `new book: TITLE`; nothing otherwise.
- `LateFeeNotifier` (name `late-fees`): for `Returned` with a fee above zero, `book ID returned late: FEE`, the fee formatted with `fees::format_cents`; nothing otherwise.
- `BorrowCounter` (name `borrows`): counts `CheckedOut` events (saturating at `u32::MAX`) and never sends a message. `count()` reads the count.

**Part 2 · The notifier**

A `Notifier` owns a `Library` and a private list of `Box<dyn Plugin>`. `register(plugin)` adds a plugin; `plugin_names()` lists them in registration order; `library()` borrows the library. `add_book`, `checkout` and `return_book` call the library's methods with the same arguments, and **only when the call succeeds** send the matching event to every plugin in registration order. Each returns the library's result together with the notifications: one `[NAME] MESSAGE` string per plugin that returned a message. A failed call sends nothing and returns the library's error. Registering a plugin doesn't replay earlier events.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: { let mut n = crate::plugins::Notifier::new(crate::Library::new()); n.register(Box::new(crate::plugins::Announcer)); n.add_book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 1965) }
Expected:   (1, ["[announcer] new book: Dune"])
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Up to 100 plugins and 1,000 events.
- No `unwrap()`, no `unsafe`.
hints: `if let Event::Added { title, .. } = event { Some(format!("new book: {title}")) } else { None }`
A private `fn emit(&mut self, event: Event) -> Vec<String>` can loop over `self.plugins.iter_mut()`, read each name, and keep the messages.
`let due = self.library.checkout(book_id, member_id, today)?;` stops before any event is sent when the checkout fails.
problems.solution_approach_md: The notifier never knows which plugins it has: it only calls `name` and `on_event` through `Box<dyn Plugin>`, so callers can register their own types. Calling the library first and using `?` means a failure returns before `emit`, so failed operations notify nobody. `Send` as a supertrait makes every boxed plugin `Send`, keeping the whole `Notifier` `Send`.
problems.idiomatic_md: A supertrait bound like `Plugin: Send` is how a trait promises properties that code holding `dyn Plugin` needs; without it, `Box<dyn Plugin>` would not be `Send`.
problems.source_checks_md: - Part 2: `Plugin` has the supertrait `Send`; `Notifier` stores `Box<dyn Plugin>` in a private field and calls `on_event`. Banned: `unwrap()`, `unsafe`.
